Good Monday afternoon. Today's newsletter, edited by Alex Fitzpatrick, is 567 words, a 2-min. read. Thanks to Bill Kole for copy editing.

 
 
1 big thing: TV networks band together
 
Photo illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Photos: Getty Images

The five major TV networks, which share responsibility for pooled video coverage of President Trump, have ceased that work in solidarity with the three outlets he banned from the White House, Axios' Sara Fischer reports.

  • ABC News, CBS News, NBC News, Fox News and CNN said in an unusual joint statement: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting."

📺 By backing CNN, MS NOW and Politico, the TV giants signaled that they're willing to use their combined leverage to pressure the White House into reinstating access.

  • The networks' power is practical and cultural: They collectively manage the pooled video that puts the presidency on television, the medium that made Trump a national celebrity and that he has long closely monitored.

🧑‍⚖️ CNN, MS NOW, and Politico today filed a joint First Amendment lawsuit, arguing that the president and his administration violated their rights by blocking access over the weekend.

  • The lawsuit is a historic show of solidarity amongst the banned outlets.

Go deeper. (Disclosure: Sara is a CNN contributor.)
 
 
2. ⛈️ El Niño triggers California statewide emergency
 
Homes damaged by flooding on Sept. 8 in Dana Point, Calif., south of Los Angeles. Photo: Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) declared a state of emergency today amid a potentially historic El Niño weather event.

  • Newsom's office says the move "directs state agencies to begin protecting vulnerable communities, prepare roads and critical infrastructure, stage emergency supplies, and help local partners reduce flood, landslide, and coastal risks."

🌊 El Niño — characterized by warmer-than-usual ocean surface temperatures in the Pacific — can drive more potent and more frequent storms and coastal flooding in California.

  • Some coastal California towns have already been dealing with erosion and property damage tied to recent storm activity.

Newsom's office noted the climate change link: "A study published in the journal Science last month found El Niño events are now more than 36% stronger than before the industrial era, with this trend accelerating over the last 40 years as the planet warms."

  • Read the announcement.

Why are gold forecasts climbing?
 
 

Global uncertainty is reshaping the gold market as Goldman Sachs Research projects the metal will reach $4,900 per troy ounce by late 2026.

This forecast is underpinned by central banks hedging against geopolitical risks as well as expectations of fewer U.S. interest rate hikes.

3. ⚡️ Catch me up
 
Screenshot: White House/YouTube
  1. 🚁 President Trump held a ribbon cutting ceremony today for his renovated White House helipad before leaving for New York and the UN General Assembly. Networks skipped the event amid the broadcast pool suspension, and the president was inaudible on the White House livestream. Go deeper.
  2. 📺 Paramount Skydance agreed to a highly anticipated settlement with 12 state attorneys general who sued to block its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The settlement clears the path for the creation of one of the biggest TV and movie behemoths in the world. More from Sara Fischer.
  3. ✈️ An equipment outage scrambled flights across the Northeast, forcing ground stops that remained ongoing as of the early afternoon. Go deeper.
 
 
4. 🛰️ 1 science thing: "Flyby" satellite pics
 
Images: HEO

Space imagery startup HEO has raised $25 million to expand into geostationary orbit, Alex Fitzpatrick reports.

📸 The company uses cameras and sensors attached to satellites to take "flyby" images of other satellites and spacecraft.

  • That lets space companies and governments better understand what's going on with their spacecraft and satellites — or those of adversarial nations.

HEO co-founder and CEO William Crowe tells Axios: "For commercial players, it allows you to really understand what's wrong with your spacecraft. So a bunch of companies have come to us when something's wrong with their spacecraft."
